items.body:
Dean Blunt’s totemic, genre-agnostic first ’Black Metal’ album is back in circulation on the heels of its killer 2nd volume, singing out a singular sort of mid-decade London blooz where his myriad circles run into one.

In 2014 ‘Black Metal’ arrived as Blunt’s 4th solo album in a string of quietly groundbreaking and guess-again solo recordings following the break-up of Hype Williams, his duo with Inga Copeland. It was an instant fave, raved about everywhere, and with the benefit of hindsight is arguably one of the past decade’s definitive highlights; a record symptomatic of the way staid generic borders were dissolving, expressing a lucid but woozy pathos that still feels timeless, yet very much of its flat-time, when the stream of musical history had pooled into the reservoir of the internet.

Returning to its slow baked charms years later ‘Black Metal’ has lost none of its allure, with a reflective stillness still belying its depths. Nimbly joining wipe clean presets and crisp licks of original instrumentation with vocals by Blunt and regular spar Joanne Robertson, their baker’s dozen tunes somehow consolidate aspects of everything from hip hop to chamber music, indie-pop to R&B with experimental wit and ohrwurming magick that places it among his most memorable and surprising records.

From the symphonic Americana lilt of ‘Lush’ to its amazing 13 minute centrepiece of chamber soul gauze ‘Forever’ and the free jazz meets folk and roadrap synthscape of ‘Grade’ it coolly piques curiosity and perplexes from every angle, resolving unfamiliar styles with a pop-sharpened manner that follows a path first taken by A.R. Kane and which quite possibly ignited a reappraisal of the problematic way in which Black music has been perceived and categorised in popular/critical culture.

All time business = unmissable.

items.body:
The Necks tantalisingly ruminate on stillness, decay and space in an absorbing, opiated follow-up to the windswept momentum of ’Travel’, chasing a quieter dragon into midnight airs shared by Loren Connors, Morton Feldman, that 'Autechre remix of Tortoise's 'To Day Retrieval', Talk Talk, Alice Coltrane.

Australia’s widely revered minimalist jazz / avant garde / electro-acoustic ambient (delete as applicable) troupe lure us right into the depths of their shared psyche with an unmissable invitation to swan the vast inner landscapes of ‘Bleed’. For an unbroken 42 minutes Chris Abrahams’ soft keys elide the shimmering plangency and distant, dreamlike drum rolls of Tony Buck and Lloyd Swanton’s painterly strokes of guitar at a seductive resting heart pace. Gently exploring notions of stasis, entropy, and space, and guided by an incandescent spirit that flickers between melancholy and the sublime, they trustingly navigate that schism with a subtlety that has propelled them since 1989’s classic ‘Sex’, and has left the template wide open for practically all Aussie experimental artists in their lustrous wake. 

Intimate yet expansive, ‘Bleed’ operates on a tongue tip of feeling in an almost palindromic arrangement that rewards repeat plays to supine minds. Chris Abrahams' grasp of extended melodic thought unfolds across the keyboard from right hand starlight to exquisitely sparing notes left to ring out on air like a syrupped Morton Feldman, gradually accreting the cross-hatching of Lloyd Swanton’s post-rock guitar hazes and bells carried on the warm air from Tony Buck, a usually ceentral figure who judiciously takes the back seat here.

Prone to leave languorous lacunæ for the imagination fills in the gaps, the piece proceeds into the most hauntingly sonorous mid section of layered, lingering overtones that hang over the atmosphere like noctilucent clouds, even precipitating a passage of atonal doom. However, they resolve via the padded palpitation of percussion at curiously bittersweet junctures in a coda that effectively leaves the keys to breeze and loop back to the start for anyone ready to go at it again. It’s typically gorgeous stuff, framing the trio at their lower case best.

items.body:
Future modal jazz dub, heard thru a Y2K lens by legendary blowers Pharaoh Sanders & Graham Haynes, and diffused in Bill Laswell’s illbient dub style & pattern. A slept-on, cross-generational ace sure to pique interest FFO Jon Hassell to Talvin Singh, Lászlo Hortobágyi to Material.

Cooked up in NYC’s jazz crucible in 2003 as a duo of Sanders & Haynes - now re-mantled as a Sanders x Laswell session for its first vinyl cut - ‘With a Heartbeat’ speaks to the rich confluence of deeply rooted, forward-thinking jazz with ambient dub that tilted from the late C.20th into this century. Centred on the human heartbeat, it unfurls at a rested systolic throb in two landscaped-scale works which bookend deeper dives into Indian raga and tabla actions, the latter of which may find favour on open-minded ‘floors, due to its effortless, toes-off-the-ground levity. But essentially, it’s idealised for floating at home or road tripping on the astral highway.

Bill Laswell’s name at the top signifies his integral input, but with no discount to Graham Hayne’s cornet, beautifully knit in warm, rising air with his peer, pioneering tenor sax player Pharaoh Sanders, who brings a half century of chops with Coltrane, Sharrock, and myriad others, to the plate. Quite simply it’s a lush listen from front to back, opening from heartical subbass pulse into 17 mins of dusted illbient dub with a cool reserve on ‘Across Time’, and shoring up in almost big beat 4th world fusion scapes reminding of the eL-Hortobãgyi Hortator album with ‘Gamaka’.

Yet we’re most partial to the midsection, where Sanders & Haynes colour the luxuriant space and rolling ballast with a wider range of brass and woodwind in the dewy raga of ‘Morning Tala’, and Trilok Gurtu’s undulating and spicy tabla and scatting vox evoke an aerial game of hashed-out kabaddi in ‘Alankara’.

items.body:
An iconic album originally brought to life via Sweden's peerless iDEAL Recordings, Kali Malone’s 'The Sacrificial Code’ is a major work featuring almost two hours of concentrated, creeping organ pieces aligned to non traditional intonation/tuning systems. It's a stunning realisation of ideas borne out of academic and conceptual rigour, with a perception-altering quality that encourages exploration without a preordained endpoint.

The Sacrificial Code’ takes a more surgical approach to the methods first explored on last year’s ‘Organ Dirges 2016 - 2017’. Over the course of three parts performed on three different organs, Malone’s minimalist process captures a jarring precision of closeness, both on the level of the materiality of the sounds and on the level of composition.The recordings here involved careful close miking of the pipe organ in such a way as to eliminate environmental identifiers as far as possible - essentially removing the large hall reverb so inextricably linked to the instrument. The pieces were then further compositionally stripped of gestural adornments and spontaneous expressive impulse -  an approach that flows against the grain of the prevailing musical hegemony, where sound is so often manipulated, and composition often steeped in self indulgence. It echoes Steve Reich’s sentiment “..by voluntarily giving up the freedom to do whatever momentarily comes to mind, we are, as a result, free of all that momentarily comes to mind.”

With its slow, purified and seemingly austere qualities ‘The Sacrificial Code’ guides us through an almost trance-inducing process where we become vulnerable receptors for every slight movement, where every miniature shift in sound becomes magnified through stillness. As such, it’s a uniquely satisfying exercise in transcendence through self restraint and by this point inarguably a modern classic.

items.body:
Carrier’s debut album features eight elegantly rude arrangements that dance in negative space between Photek’s frictional syncopations, Rhythm & Sound’s dubwise minimalism and Torsten Pröfrock’s fractured dynamics, bolstered on two tracks by contributions from Voice Actor & Memotone, summoning a noirish, jazzier frisson to his signature metrics and temporalities.

Since hard-snagging our ears and feet in 2023 with 12”s for FELT and his own eponymous label, Guy Brewer’s Carrier has become the go-to project for anyone who had almost given up on chasing these sort of ultra-subtle but vitally distinctive new permutations in dance music. For the past two years, his unpredictable variations within a style have kept us all tip-toed and seat-edged with organisations of a finely chiselled percussive palette and smouldering ambient noise that distills the salient aspects and spirits of D&B, dub techno, electro-acoustic music and trip hop with unique traction. In effect, he’s enacted a clear leap of imagination from previous work issued as part of Commix and solo as Shifted that only continues to reveal hallucinatory psychoacoustics on this first album detail. 

‘Rhythm Immortal’ sees Brewer tilt the project into slower, resoundingly more atmospheric realms, better to luxuriate in the instinctive guile and integer-stepping style ’n pattern of his incredible sound. At the album’s poles, a vocal cameo by cult gynoid Voice Actor follows from Gavsborg’s on a preceding 7” single to ideally model his sound’s mutability and compatibility with trip hop forms, and Memotone helps seal the deal with a hovering glow lent to ‘Offshore’, whilst Carrier jostles the reins throughout with masterful control of his thing, crisply purposed to the album canvas. In that context, it’s perfectly adaptable to bodies both supine or in motion, ushering a hypnagogic sway with ‘A Point Most Crucial’, and hingeing around the slightest interplay of 16th note hi-hat ruffles and recoiling reverbs on ‘Outer Shell’, or blissfully stepping on knife-edge 2-step on ‘Wave After Wave’. 

The album conveys a deeply personal pulse and spiritual devotion to that kind of all-tension-no-release mode typical of so much music we love - from Kode9’s earliest re-factoring of Prince to Photek’s ‘Ni-Ten-Ichi-Ryu’, from T++/Dynamo and Traktor’s asymmetric dynamics to Burial’s shockout debut - refactored with a rare conviction in its unspoken powers to activate the eyes-shut imagination. Unmissable stuff.

items.body:
Quietly unheimlich, slowcore dream-pop transformations of Western and Japanese kids’ music by a nascent Osaka duo for Em Records...

"The terms “nursery rhymes” and “children’s songs” may give rise to visions of idyllic innocence and the charms of childhood, but Play Nursery Rhymes and Children's Songs brings forth quite different aural imagery: this is an eerie and unsettling sonic picture book which hints at the darkness and mystery which form the hidden heart of many traditional songs and rhymes. The length of the songs provides a hint: each piece delves deeply into the latent uncanniness of the music, with superficial innocence gradually displaced as electric guitar, bass, field recordings and concrete sounds draw the listener into a chilly forest, while Tokiyo Ooto’s voice croons dark “lullabies for adults,” blending elements of folk, slowcore and dream pop.

The Tokiyo Ooto & Orhythmo duo formed in 2023, releasing their first album in 2024. This release updates two pieces from the first album, and also includes a traditional Japanese children’s song from Shiga Prefecture and a masterpiece for children by composer Yasushi Akutagawa. Both musicians are Osaka-based: Otoo is a guitarist and singer-songwriter who also works in band and solo contexts; Orhythmo is a bassist with hardcore punk roots who focuses on improvisation, drone, noise and ambient sound."

Príncipe outliers Niagara slosh across the grid on a 76 minute tape of free-flowing deep, acidic house and offbeat, organismic techno marinaded in briny Drexciyan synth substance and a sort of worming, villalobos-y ecstasy.

As with the trio’s previous pair of LPs, the cassette format proves an ideal canvas to showcase Niagara’s peculiar sound in long form. Through seamless but asymmetric transitions that run like a mixtape, they stitch myriad productions with a knotty intuition best to represent their unique bent on club hydrodynamics and hypnosis honed over the course of dozens of releases since 2013. 

For the locked-in duration they remind us of E.R.P./Convextion or the flow of NWAQ in the album’s absorbing arrangement of lissom, insistent grooves and harmonised synth colours that feel as though they naturally occur and bleed, ribboning into each next piece for holistic immersion. 

The first side trots to a steady 120 pace propelled by breezy pads dusted  thru subaquatic caverns of light-bending melody and passages reminding us of Kassem Mosse via Actress in their coarse traction, or even Jamal Moss at his most reflective, ultimately shoring up in weightless but forward pulses. The B-side picks up the tempo to a thrumming Detroit techno velocity akin to the recent Howard Thomas album or classic Rob Hood , maintaining the pressure with a slinky, refined guile that sounds like a recall of times well spent in the dance.

Both tunes sound very much of their time, when European techno was forged tougher to demand, paralleling movements of harder Chicago house and Detroit warehouse techno.

In Panasonic’s case, the results were typically ascetic, mostly bleached of discernible melody beyond rhythmelodic cadence, and locked, bloody-minded, to icy tattoos that reflected their origins in Finnish warehouse parties, and would pin them on the international techno and electronic music maps. Trust that ‘Muuntaja’ still leaves welts from its distorted kicks, and contains subs primed to quake foundations, whilst the B-side is ideal for gnashing rave punks and bass drum fetishists.

items.body:
Death Is Not The End return to the soul-stir sound of deep south Sacred Harp Singers in 1993 - although it could feasibly be any time since the advent of portable tape recording - in the blessed company of the Union Grove Baptist Church, Ozark, Alabama. Feels just right in this humidity…

The Wiregrass Singers' Dewey Williams began learning the shape-note tradition in his childhood. He studied under Judge Jackson, who authored the landmark 1934 hymnbook The Colored Sacred Harp. In 1971, Williams formally organized The Wiregrass Sacred Harp Singers to preserve the music full-time. This unified troupe began touring nationally and leading workshops, which ultimately launched them onto stages at the Smithsonian and Newport folk festivals up until Williams' passing in 1995 when the group disbanded. The African-American Sacred Harp tradition in the Wiregrass region has steeply declined since the start of the 21st century, due to an aging generation of singers, and today it is largely sustained through archival preservation and occasional multi-book singing meetups.

This raw recording, made at the Union Grove Baptist Church, Ozark in mid-April 1993 finds the group singing from B. F. White’s The Sacred Harp (1844), which together with his brother-in-law William Walker’s Southern Harmony (1835) formed the musical backbone of generations of Southern music and Southern musical styles.

items.body:
Anyone charmed by Anvar Kalandarov’s Silk Road mixes will be all over this return ticket to Central Asian Synthesisers, spotlighting a general blindspot of ’80s-‘90s Uzbek & Tajik disco for Western ears...

On the leather loafer heels of ‘Digging Central Asia: Musical Archeology Along The Silk Road’, collector and archivist qorakitobchi aka Anvar Kalandarov returns to a region known as historic, transcontinental crossroads, at a point when it transitioned from Soviet rule to relative independence. The music reflects its Central Asian provenance with a blend of Western disco, as filtered via Soviet modernity, inflected with a melodic sweetness that our untrained ears affiliate with Chinese pop, and film and pop music of Pakistan and the subcontinent, or in other words; a rarified pleasure for those with a sweet tooth for disco frivolity.

Kalandarov and Death Is Not the End’s exquisite ear for enduring tunes is fully locked in across both sides. The first gets into gear with cooing divas strapped to vestiges of late ‘70s disco, flush with microtonal synth plumes, before steadily edging into ’80s disco pomp, proper, and a big old Euro-house belter. The other side follows into more surprising, off-road oddities ranging from a bit of spiky new wave synth funk to racier Eurasian NRG and flashdance panache, paving the way to a big romantic ballad and a closing starburst of peak time Euro-house to seal the deal.

items.body:
Psych duo Bear Bones, Lay Low naturally adapt to soundtrack dimensions with a richly atmospheric, electroacoustic accompaniment to Léonard Pongo’s titular film, benefitting from Laszlo Umbreit’s experience in this arena.

“Discrepant presents the LP edition of Tales from the Source, the original film soundtrack by Bear Bones, Lay Low and Laszlo Umbreit. Originally composed for Belgian-Congolese artist Léonard Pongo’s 2024 film of the same name, this release reworks the film's audio into a continuous, fluid listening experience.

The album is built on a direct contrast between heavy electronic manipulation and raw environmental audio. Laszlo Umbreit captured the foundation of the record through field recordings and additional electronics, focusing on the quiet, tactile sounds of water, riverbeds, and natural spaces. These recordings were then processed and expanded by Bear Bones, Lay Low, who layered the tracks using synthesizers, samplers and various effects processors.

Rather than acting as a standard background score, the music functions as a detailed piece of environmental sound art. The tracks are edited to blend into one another without distinct gaps, mirroring the slow pace and visual flow of the film. Through the use of tape loops, filtering, and electronic processing, the natural landscapes are systematically distorted and rearranged. The result is a dark, slow-moving suite of electroacoustic music that strips away traditional melody to focus entirely on texture, resonance, and the changing dynamics of the recorded environments.”

Class vinyl debut of Lee ‘Scratch’ Perry’s live band bass player, Slim Levy, trading in charmingly dare-to-differ cosmic dub sorcery on an ideal home for this type of lark - Disrupt’s indomitable Jahtari.

Aside to private dubplates, ’Snippet Sounds’ is the French multi-instrumentalist’s first record, proper; a carousel of gently psychoactive and subtle skews on convention that chimes with soundsystema nd dub outliers such as Sheriff Lindo or Tapes, or the rest of the of the Jahtari kru, for that matter. 

Taking equal cues from his former bandleader (he played on Perry’s last tour), and The Beach Boys’ ‘Pet Sounds’, the set reels to 14 succinct and DJ-ready parts, dancing between toytronic vignettes and more fully formed knees-ups that echo the strange, innovative spectres of ‘70s Black Ark output via more lo-fi tekkerz.

To play favourites, we advise checking for the plucky, air-step skank of ‘Chalaladub’, the rickety ‘Chim Cherie’ vintage vibe of ‘Characteristics’ and ‘Train Train’, or perfectly sozzled drunken master style of ‘The Evil Cowboy Condor’, thru the early digickal bubbler ‘Wake Up John’. But ultimately we reckon it’s best taken in one go, where the tidgier bits come into their own in an album context.

items.body:
First time reissue of Wolfgang Voigt's foundational first GAS album since its release in 1996 - it remains the archetype for so much contemporary ambient music and back-room techno, melting camouflaged German cultural references into a timeless, anthemic pulse. This new reissue is the original extended vinyl version, with definitive longer versions of the six classic tracks. Available in deluxe 3LP and single CD editions.

By the mid-'90s, techno had become the language of German youth culture, tied up in the country's long history of electronic musical innovation - from Kluster to Kraftwerk - and the revolutionary cry of reunification when the Berlin Wall fell in 1989. Based in Köln, Voigt had already put his stamp on dance music by the time he embarked on the mysterious GAS project, working alongside his brother Reinhard to help devise the sound that would evolve into minimal techno, but GAS felt different - more illusory, hypnotic. 

The name, aside from accurately describing the vaporous ambience that whispers through each track, stands for Germany, Austria, Switzerland, and it was Voigt's concept to not only express the feeling of dropping acid in the Königsforst, a verdant woodland only a short drive from Köln, but to distill centuries of German music into a contemporary haze that reflected a hopeful new era. And after testing the waters with '95's Profan-released EP 'Modern', Voigt set a new benchmark with 'GAS', laying out his narrative over six long movements, the shortest of which clocks in at just under 12 minutes.

Voigt wasn't interested in making songs, exactly, but emphasizing texture, burying samples of traditional German music - from baroque to schlager - in murky drones punctuated by squashed 4/4 rhythms. Not dance music exactly, it's headphone gear that's referencing the dance canon in its shift from the US, through Jamaica and the UK to Germany. Much like the Artificial Intelligence era in the UK, it imprints the familiar cycles (pulsing kick drums, undulating soundsystem-ready basslines) with its own regional character. It's no mistake that Voigt begins with an entirely beatless composition that paints the landscape without revealing the complete palette. The album's airiest track, 'GAS 1' is a stylistic milestone - something we can hear tracking thru electronic music from then until now; just listen to Jan Jelinek, Vladislav Delay, PAN's 'Mono No Aware' comp, or anything on the West Mineral imprint. It's ambient music, but where Eno's vision was trained on an earlier era, Voigt had cut his teeth on acid house, hardcore and Detroit techno, and was able to muddle those influences with his own homegrown obsessions. 

That famous, omnipresent filtered kick makes its first appearance on 'GAS 2', thudding beneath watery glitches and sweeping orchestral pads. Voigt doesn't make his concept too vivid (at least at this stage in its evolution), but the outline of classical music is there, punctured by mesmerising minimal thuds that as yet hadn't become a meme. It's not music that develops, it exists, freezing a moment in time and letting the mind pick out a scene, concentrating on the organic, shifting harmonies rather than the static beat. If acid house was all about the squelch, this was all about vapour, as sample-rich pads seem to disappear into clouds of static, blooming from the density. There's a more evident schlager-inspired swing on 'GAS 4' that Voigt and his Kompakt crew would explore more in the coming years, but it's contorted into a subterranean rumble, and on 'GAS 5', the producer tentatively glances trance's quivering euphoria, using reverb and delay to turn anthemic stabs into whooshing melodic rushes. 

If you haven't managed to hear GAS before, this is the perfect starting point, and if you've only heard the album in its truncated form (both the CD release and the 'Nah und Fern' version were incomplete), then we've got to say this is the one.

Whewwww!!! Titans in their fields Mark Fell & Pat Thomas induce proper hyper-jazz screwfaces with some of the rudest, most adventurous tackle in either’s arsenal. Wigs will be flipped! 

In mid March, 2025, on their first recorded encounter, Mark Fell & Pat Thomas split and reengineered the electro-jazz atom at Sheffield Uni’s Firth Hall. Just a week prior we had the pleasure of catching Thomas shred jazz standards with vocalist Elaine Mitchener in a Whalley Range church, before Thomas notably leaned into a section of ruggeder, more rhythmic electronics, as he’s prone to do. It would appear here that that unerring thrust toward warping synthetic tones is flipped on its swede as the august pianist knows exactly what to do with Fell’s swarm of cutlery workshop prongs and whirring algorithmic ructions harnessed in ‘Reality Is Not A Theory’, where Fell’s astonishingly free - yet acutely disciplined - maelstrom of attack and buzz meets its match in Thomas’ adroit whirlwind of discordant, clustered chords and ambidextrous keyboard punishments. 

A masterclass in playing your own game on both sides of the equation, ‘Reality Is Not A Theory’ is initially mannered but ultimately driven by a clinamen of chaos in a frankly fucking sexy style. Both approach the session at arguably a peak of their powers and sense of freeness, appearing to prowl, stalk each other, conversing in terse jabs and storm-brew doom chords with shards of percussion flying from oblique angles in the sound stage for the opening half of the first side. But when they appear to get the measure of each other, dialling it right down to near silence, and samurai-wielded, shakuhachi-like swoop and skull-clock donk, it’s night night for the next 30 minutes with a straight K.O. of asymmetric musical pugilism. 

Of course they’re both surely lovely guys, wouldn’t hurt a fly, but the sense of two prize fighters sparring is palpable as the piece tilts between its staccato skirmishes, spasmodic rolls, and almost drill-type trills or blasts beats, countered with low-end keyboard undercuts and complex chord ambushes in jaw-dropping motion. What emerges is an uncompromising, alloyed ideal of Fell's interests in the contradictions of “multistability” and Thomas’ unfathomable modal tekkerz, with the former pushing the clarity of synth-pop, techno and glitch’s distinctive pulses with singular ductility, and the latter pushed to respond - or vice-versa - in a likewise unique vernacular that steps off from free jazz, Arabic and minimalist classical into genuinely thrilling, polymetric, 3D space-time of conflict and resolution. Trust you’ll need a whole pack of Marlboro reds after this ravishing session, whether you smoke or not.

items.body:
Enigmatic label/collective life is beautiful fully establishes its lore on a colossal 3LP sprawl: 39 tracks of whimsical outsider biz arcing from lo-fi strums to asymmetric pop, jazz improv, poetry, noise, abstract hip-hop, spoken word and whatever else captures the thing, from artists you'll know and a fair few you won’t, featuring Bianca Scout, aloisius, VOICE ACTOR, James Massiah, Kenichi Iwasa, THE NARRATOR, Isaiah Hull, Pretty V and many, many more.

A self-styled gesamtkunstwerk, life is beautiful was established by aloisius in 2022 as a radio show, before turning into a collective, a series of live performances, and then inevitably a record label a year later. Their first comp makes some attempt to pull all their various strands into something cohesive, but like many of the best collectives - Mica Levi’s Curl crew for example - so much of the beauty and joy comes from following the breadcrumb trail deep into wherever they take you. This is a label, after all, that dumped their demos and experiments ("resources and inspiration") on a file exchange portal on their own site, so you get the idea that nothing is quite fixed, and there are no easy answers - just the pleasure of tagging along for the ride.

The set opens with tracks from each of the founders, who establish the label's core sound. NWAKKE begins with 'i need you in a positive way', a cloudy hypnagogic R&B marvel that juxtaposes cool-headed vocal runs with tape-fucked field recordings and piano. Then, the mic's handed to Amber Joy, aka THE NARRATOR, who also serves as the label's artistic director; on 'SUDDENLY', she oozes a skittish post-everything collage that chops cheap synths and choral vocals into a dreamy modern hymn. aloisus' 'you are god' runs out of its stuck groove as if it emerges from the very same thought, blurring gospel moans across LinnDrum loops. Bianca Scout hands us a taster of her collaborative work with London's Cajm on the hypnotic 'Welcome to Hello', while poet Isaiah Hull teams up with y+Your for the wonked 'vampire money'.

Basically there's a whole record of music from the crew before 'veneration...' even begins in earnest, and it only gets better from here, running through aesthetic experiments from multi-instrumentalist Kenichi Iwasa, self-styled "beat wizard" psychedelic ensemble. (who's one half of Brum's Everything is Psychedelic with Tony Bontana) and Thom Dehli before we reach the compilation's crown jewel, a 21-minute live jam from okk70 ensemble. We can't tell you exactly who's playing, but it's worth the price of entry alone, a squirming slo-mo jazz side that gets to the roots of the life is beautiful sound - like some cross between ’87 era Prince and Oren Ambarchi’s Ghosted Trio, except deep in the basement. Elsewhere, there's a chewably eccentric solo moment from Bianca Scout ('superscribe 24'), a phenomenally moody collaboration between VOICE ACTOR and aloisius ('24'), a spirited, lo-fi transmission from London's josiane pozi and a deeper than deep jam from orchestra379, aloisius' "collective improvisation project" that's featured artists like Ben Vince, Kenichi Iwasa and abi asisa. 

Label comps are often a slog but this one's stuffed to the gills with genuinely creative experimentation from some of the scene's most interesting outsiders, the sprawl really does come close to harnessing the vibe.

Field Records’ treasured Monolake reissue program yields a first vinyl cut of the influential project’s 2nd album - the last as a duo of Robert Henke & Gerhard Behles, before the latter turned attention wholly to developing Ableton Live software. Genuine landmark stuff for electronica fiends

In suit with the reissued ‘Hong Kong’ (1997) comp of early EPs for Chain Reaction, and the self-released debut LP ‘Gravity’ (2001), comes ‘Interstate’; one of Monolake’s most distinctive entries in the space where dub techno met concrète sound design and hypermodern electronica. The 65 minute album sees Henke & Behles ultimately conclude a vision of a semi-organic techno architecture that transcends club, home, and can listening, thanks to their judicious balance of whirring, syncopated grooves and custom-built, elemental sound design that feels remarkably future-proofed, then and now, 

In historic terms the duo follow a line of activated electronic systems from David Tudor to Lee “Scratch” Perry, Vince Clarke to Uwe Schmidt, Basic Channel and Autechre, by breathing vivid, imaginary life and space into circuitry and code. More specifically, in Monolake’s hands, everything teems with insectoid detail and a fascinating depth perception, conjuring immersive environments one can take as much pleasure from dancing to as simply admiring its elegantly awesome architexture. 

The relatively new freedoms of Max/MSP software and the pair’s ever heightened proprioception allowed them to enact forms of impossible physics that dance into hyperspace between the air-stepping lushness of ‘abundance’ and needlepoint D&B abstractions ‘ginza’ or ‘terminal’, showcasing sheer, advanced tekkerz on ‘gecko’ and serving the ‘floor with nexx-level depths on two parts of ‘tangent’, plus the metallic electro ping-pong of ‘perpetuum’ and 10 mins of proto-virtual reality in ‘amazon.’

Wah Wah Wino​'s Davy Kehoe, Morgan Buckley and Olmo are joined by avant legend Roger Doyle, among others, on a delectably brilliant, 54 minute collage, re-upped with new artwork for 2026.

An ode to the putative pleasures of ketamine, ‘KWALK’ emulates the effect of everyone’s fave equine dissociative with a mazy disarray of folk rock, ambient electronics and balmy, bandy-legged grooves bent for getting ketty with it. Inside, song structures quiesce to smeared samples and fractal lines of thought perhaps familiar to anyone who’s done a bump or two.

As with all WIno joints, normal logic is out the window, replaced by a loosey goosey slant that's a real pleasure to follow. In their slippery snakes ’n ladders chicanery, ‘KWALK’ recalls everything from Davy Kehoe's endlessly-rinsed 'Storm Desmond' to the Lost Highway OST, The KLF’s 'Chill Out' to Sigtryggur Berg Sigmarsson & BJ NIlsen’s ‘Avantgardegasse’ ace thru to Don Cherry’s communal free jazz jams and Laura Cannell’s folk flights in our minds, and should be considered a go-to slab for those times when the sofa’s on the ceiling and everyone’s too munted to pick another tune.

We have a special place in our hearts for mixtapes/collage pieces pressed to vinyl - and this one is prob the best we've heard since John T. Gast's 'Invocations II' set for Blowing Up The Workshop a few years back.

items.body:
The momentous Chain Reaction full-length debut by Robert Henke and Gerhard Behles aka Monolake, issued on vinyl for the very first time on its 25th anniversary and still sounding as sleekly futuristic as ever.

Replete in its definitive remastered edition, which features additional field recordings of rain and insects on ‘Cyan’, Monolake’s debut album is a masterclass of late ‘90s techno straddling widescreen ambient soundscapes and pulsing, Berlin-standard dub techno. It gathers tracks from 1996’s preceding 12” releases, ‘Cyan’, ‘Lantau /Macao’, and ‘Occam / Arte’ plus ‘Index’ from his Helical Scan project, in a landmark album that, with hindsight, can be heard as a milestone between early ‘90s ambient techno and subsequent, sleeker forms of minimalism and spatialized sound design that reflected and deeply influenced techno and electronic music to come.

The re-edit of ‘Cyan’, teeming with insectoid nanorhythms and the patter of rain, opens a seminal set that distills the head-long energy of ‘90s techno to a blissful sublime without losing its vital propulsion. In the tunnelling dynamic of ‘Index’ thru the exquisitely light-footed stepper ‘Occam’ he conceives a sort of techno purism comparable with Basic Channel but distinguished by its relatively crisp contours and HD definition. But he also proves equally adept at other routes and branches of techno, as with the slow, heaving designs of ‘Lantau / Macau’, which impressionistically convey his times spent in the Far East through mutated field recordings, while the radiant ‘Arte’ is a masterpiece of downtempo ambient techno, and ‘Mass Transit Railway’ ropes in fellow synth fiend Wieland Samolak, who wrote user manuals and their translations for Emu Systems and Sequential Circuits - for a floating high-water mark of ‘90s ambient ambient sound design.

items.body:
The Genioh Yamashirogumi collective, most famous for 1988's Symphonic Suite Akira, feature on this incredible 1986 album that shares much of Akira's musical DNA with expansive orchestrations performed by more than 200 musicians and taking in Tibetan horns, Bulgarian-style chorales, rhythmelodic gamelan and central African field recordings rich with hypersonic frequencies​.

Undoubtedly the most vital reissue of the year, 'Ecophony Rinne' is the precursor to 1988's iconic 'Symphonic Suite Akira' - and to our minds is even better. The sheer ambition here is remarkable, smashing together thousands of years of culture and nascent technology, collaborating with literally hundreds of musicians and figuring a blueprint for experimental music that's rarely properly examined.

We know you've heard the 'Akira' soundtrack. And we still remember catching it for the first time, wondering why its future-ancient sounds - Baleinese gamelan orchestra chimes, Japanese noh chants, baroque chorals and unsettling synthesized elements - worked so well with the sci-fi milestone's viscerally affecting post-apocalyptic themes. To Katsuhiro Otomo, the music was never an afterthought: it had been developed before the film had even been figured out; the rhythm of the action is utterly in debt to Geinoh Yamashirogumi's innovative score. And we can follow those roots directly to 'Ecophony Rinne', an album that appeared to little fanfare (in the West, at least) back in 1986. The man behind the project was Dr. Tsutomu Ōhashi, an agricultural scientist, composer and prestigious author who's better known, at least in musical circles, by his pseudonym Shoji Yamashiro. When he was at university, he studied microbiology, but he found himself drawn to music in parallel, learning Western-style conducting and working with the Hato no Kai student choir in the 1960s. And it was this experience that led him to question Western musical logic; he saw the limitations of the system, founding Geinoh Yamashirogumi in 1974 as a reaction - an opportunity to share his radically open-minded sonic philosophy with curious minds in his community.

Yamashiro avoided "classically-trained" musicians, preferring to work with amateurs who enjoyed music's instinctual qualities as much as he did - and he refused to box himself into a single culture's creative output. He didn't actively avoid the Western canon, but he didn't focus on it either, examining Indonesian folk music, Hindustani forms, Bulgarian choral music and African indigenous traditions with the same breathless energy. In fact, it was during a trip to the Democratic Republic of Congo, where he lived with the Mbuti peoples in the Ituri Rainforest, when the seeds of 'Ecophony Rinne' were sown. Yamashiro realized that the Mbuti's improvised polyphonic music, made completely without scores or schools, was just as complex as the renaissance choral music he'd studied at college. This revelation backed up the ideas that had driven him to found Geinoh Yamashirogumi in the first place and when he returned to Japan, he began to develop a suite that didn't concentrate on a single aspect of music or even pure sound itself, fixating on the harmonies that bring together millennia of evolution. This wasn't world music, it was human music that attempted to work completely outside of the usual hierarchies.

Of course, something this ambitious wouldn't work unless it was reined in masterfully, and that's where Yamashiro really excels. If you've heard 'Symphonic Suite Akira', you'll already recognize the general aesthetic, but it's the scope of 'Ecophony Rinne' that puts it in its own bracket. It's too vague to call it cinematic, even; we get a general feeling of scope from the immense, teeming soundscapes, constructed meticulously by Yamashiro from the work of literally hundreds of collaborators, field recordings he collected throughout the world and samples he'd been archiving for years, but it's because his sonic references have been used by other since the release of 'Ecophony Rinne' and 'Symphonic Suite Akira' that we hear it as such a relatable narrative. When it was released, there was simply nothing else like it - a true polyphonic experience that treats different elements like shades of color, brushing rhythmelodic Balinese gamelan sequences next to screeching birds and insects captured in the rainforest, references to Bach and Beethoven as well as Balkan folk choirs and processed kosmische synths. It's breathtaking, impossible even to absorb in a single sitting - we realize we harp on about deep listening, but occasionally a close, focused session is all that will do a record justice.

It doesn't even stop there; when Yamashiro was checking the test pressing for the album, he noticed that the vinyl version sounded much better than the digital files and wanted to know exactly why. So of course, he enlisted a team of listeners and hooked them up to medical equipment to test their brainwaves. He realized that because CDs usually had the sound rolled off at 22.05kHz, there were seemingly inaudible ultra-high frequencies being lost that were crucial to the experience - sounds that would be found naturally in verdant environments and sounds that make gamelan orchestras so undeniably rich. He dubbed this "the hypersonic effect" and established Studio Terra, a fidelity research lab, to develop special speakers to replicate the proper sound of the music. Thankfully, for anyone with a good set of speakers, this new reissue, the first proper one since its original release four decades ago, has been treated with the respect it deserves, mastered at half-speed at Abbey Road and handled with 'nuff care so that the frequencies are preserved. You might not be able to hear it, but you fully feel that there's something special happening - we'd even say that 'Ecophony Rinne' is one of the most prescient, most innovative records of the 1980s. Essential doesn't come close.

items.body:
The fourth LP from Skyjack — the borderless five piece band spread across South Africa and Switzerland.

"Recorded in December 2025 at a secluded studio outside Stellenbosch, South Africa, the album captures the vibrant live energy of the band at its most expansive — drawing together free improvisation, South African jazz traditions, chamber music, kinetic groove, and ecstatic collective interplay into a singular body of work.

“This record is a very articulate representation of our sound, having grown deep roots into the earth with high branches reaching upward and outward”, says bassist Shane Cooper. “My desire is always to create sonic universes that can envelope the listener.”

The album’s title comes from a line in a poem by the 13th-century Persian poet Rumi, reflecting the music’s balance between groundedness and transcendence. Here, Skyjack move fluidly between meditative improvisation and lush orchestration across twelve tracks of free-spirited, cosmic journeying. Inspired both by the cultural traditions and natural environments of South Africa, Let The Sky Open Under Your Feet is a testament to the band’s intuitive connection and innate musical curiosity.

It arrives just over a year after Light Cycle (2024), a short gap that reflects the momentum built on tour. After exchanging sketches remotely across two continents, the band reunited in Johannesburg in late 2025, workshopped the new material onstage across South Africa, and then headed directly into the studio, where much of the album was recorded live in first takes — preserving the looseness and unpredictability central to Skyjack’s sound.

Comprised of Kyle Shepherd (piano), Shane Cooper (bass), Jonno Sweetman (drums), Andreas Tschopp (trombone), and Marc Stucki (saxophones), Skyjack first formed in Cape Town in 2013 during a fertile moment in South African jazz, as a new generation of musicians pushed against rigid genre definitions and opened the music outward toward broader sonic possibilities. Over the past decade, the band has built a singular sound drawing equally on South African groove traditions and European improvisation.

Individually, the members move between jazz, electronic music, film scoring, rock, hip-hop and experimental composition, with collaborations spanning artists including William Parker, Lionel Loueke, Zim Ngqawana, Ben LaMar Gay, Jorge Rossy, Shabaka Hutchings, William Kentridge, Makaya McCraven and Sylvie Courvoisier.

Since their self-titled debut in 2015, followed by The Hunter (2019) and Light Cycle (2024), the group has developed a reputation for immersive live performances and music that continuously reshapes itself in motion — rooted in what they describe as “warm menacing African grooves,” while refusing fixed stylistic borders."

items.body:
Without question, some of the most absorbing music you'll likely ever hear, compiled in a 4 hour-long triple disc set.

'Fremde Zeit - Addendum' collects five pieces of etheric, liminal composition by Jakob Ullmann (1958), the widely acknowledged master of Quiet music.  For us, as we'd imagine many others, it's a striking first introduction to the German minimalist's very particular body of work. Comprising 4 hours of barely-there strings, percussions, wind instruments and voices prefaced by the instruction "Please choose, for each piece, the volume settings of your sound system so as to just barely mask the ambient sounds in the room", this is music made for concentrated listening, recorded and specifically designed to give listeners "the opportunity to hear more, and better" by the simple but essential notion that "We hear better because we make an effort to hear better."

With this is mind, we're invited into a sound world which actively, yet effortlessly challenges our perceptions of space and time with a compelling, transcendent effect akin to that of listening to music by, say, Eliane Radigue or Morton Feldman, yet with an alien, detached appeal entirely its own. Due to their extended durations - no piece is shorter than 34 mins, and over an hour at the longest - we form temporal impressions which blur the boundaries between our immediate space and the apparent vastness of the recording, teasing our sixth sense to wander on a knife edge of trepidation and somnolence.

Once you've heard this music it should come as little surprise Ullmann studied sacred music in Dresden from 1979-1982 - his music could be the lingering resonance of an Arvo Pärt piece played in a huge cathedral, carrying the weight of history.

A revelatory package, whose impact will surely emerge and manifest as slowly, yet powerfully, as the music itself.

In physical stature and imaginative scope, Luc Ferrari’s 10 x CD / 11 Hour selection for INA GRM’s series presents a poetic building block of C.20th electronic music from the founding director of the GRM in 1958, presenting a unique art history spanning six decades of ingenious, beguiling soundcraft.

Part of a legendary series including titles by concrète pioneers Pierre Schaefer & Pierre Henry, plus weighty surveys of Bernrad Parmegiani, Éliane Radigue and François Bayle, this lavish boxset of Luc Ferrari’s work is a masterclass exploration of avant garde form and function that charts experimental music’s research and development during a radical phase. While even the notion of such a large storage device for sound was unimaginable when Ferrari began making his cut-up musical collages and sound poetry in the ‘50s, his ‘L’Œuvre Électronique’ covers the progression of musical technology and thought from its most laboriously executed origins, working with tape and raw blocks of sound, to the grander digital staging of his ‘90s and early ‘00s radio plays, plotted for multiple voices and spatialised landscapes. 

Collected, this set forms an incredible deep dive into art-music history where the materiality of sound is questioned and reconsidered in relief of its musical connotations, creating in the process a peerless body of work that better approximates the texture of dreams or the audness of waking life than any song, and has long informed the approach to sound organisation by a host of progressive artists, effectively bridging the conceptual precedents of Varèse and Cage and the contemporary futures projected by Lee Gamble or Valerio Tricoli.

The 98 tracks from 31 releases, clocking up just over 10 hours of recordings, delineate across decades following Ferrari’s studies with Messaien and Honegger in the mid ‘50s, and a period of illness that made him better acquainted with the radio receiver, and pioneers such as Schöneberg and Webern, to his co-founding of the Groupe de Recherches Musicales with Schaeffer and François-Bernard Mâche in 1958, and thru his landmark transformation of field recordings made on a Yugoslavian beach, and the ravishing abstractions of later electronic works. 

Until his passing, aged 76 in Arezzo, Italy, Ferrari remained ceaselessly active both in his own practice and teaching, and was revered as the poet of musique concrète. He bought a particularly gallic purview to the paradigm, especially when considered against the more hard-nosed academic pursuits of his peers, making singular use of vocals as an elusive or sometimes literal presence in his works in a way that others didn’t, and as such his works all hare a certain liminal quality that appears richly seductive to fans of fantasy storytelling as much as psychedelic soundtracks and sound as dreamfood imagery.

Chicago soul-jazz prodigy and sax player Isaiah Collier hits Stevie Wonder levels of unbridled joy on his debut EP with Gilles Peterson and co.’s label...

“In a world currently defined by unrest, uncertainty, and cultural fracture, acclaimed saxophonist, composer, and bandleader Isaiah Collier returns with Joy, a 5-track EP that reframes one of humanity’s most nuanced emotions both as a devotional grounding and political act.

Collier’s deeply personal compositions present joy as an act that isn’t rooted in escapism or abstraction, but rather, as something hard-won rooted in lived experience, shaped by transformation, and sustained through connection. Throughout the album’s five compositions, Collier positions joy as a guiding light during challenging times, an expression of challenging yourself to utilize your gifts, an affirmation of love and discovery, and as an affirmative source of reassurance.”

Key Chicago house architect Ron Trent departs the club for the bedroom under new alias La Marr, a new vent for his most romantic, sublime soundscapes, warmly advised FFO Detroit Escalator Company, Terre Thaemlitz, Wally Badarou, Klaus Schulze, MvO Trio

Light candles/incense and scatter petals for optimal effect when immersing in La Marr’s debut ‘Mood Programs’ EP, which finds a perfect home nestled amid Music From Memory’s precious, timeline-twining cuts of new age ambient, kosmiche, and Balearic wist. It’s also a natural, logical progression from the sort of depths usually secreted in Trent’s albums, but here given full sides to unfurl their functions, which we’re sure will also sound dead tasty, syrupy slow, on 33-not-45. 

He paints the lushest 12 min panorama of elliptical stereo pads, floating organ cloud structures and skin-stroke arps in ‘Good Magic’, edging on similar terrain to Terre Thaemlitz’s golden revision of Tangerine Dream’s ‘Love on a Real Train’, where a fine line of hand played drums emphasises the swaying groove - swooning either bed-ways or a little rug-cut, depending on your disposition - before ‘Clear’ hustles a palette of the slinkiest Afro-Latinate, Brazilian rhythms under big, dusky skies, hinting at Manuel Göttsching via MvO Trio. 

Your ears do not deceive you: this one is proper lush.

Oren Ambarchi's kraut-techno-free jazz magnum opus is back for its 10th anniversary -  an ambitious ensemble piece featuring an all-star list of players including Ricardo Villalobos, Keith Fullerton Whitman, Mark Fell, crys Cole, Will Guthrie, Arto Lindsay and Konrad Sprenger... Wooooo

You've got to admire Ambarchi's chutzpah here. 'Hubris' is an all you can eat buffet of his various musical cravings, a chance for his friends, influences and collaborators to flex a little and for Ambarchi to attempt to ride the groove like an experienced cowboy on an out-of-control bucking bronco. The first side is the biggest surprise, a dedication to Wang Chung's enduring, disco-influenced 'To Live and Die in L.A.' soundtrack that begins with ping-ponging guitar notes and Jim O'Rourke's synth blips, before elusive Berlin-based composer Konrad Sprenger (aka Joerg Hiller) drops in with some motorized guitar vamps. It's rhythmic gear that fits in with the Berlin school until Mark Fell appears in the final third with some typically fractured percussion.

On the flip, the groove loosens after a short guitar interlude. Ricardo Villalobos takes over with a suitably winding, minimal throb over live rhythms played by Joe Talia and Will Guthrie simultaneously as krautrock techno mutates into disco fusion. Keith Fullerton Whitman tries to nudge the track off the rails with his modular expositions, but the path is set - Arto Lindsay's axe is just the icing on the cake. By the end of the side, we're in full jazz-noise mode: everything's still pegged to Villalobos' central pulse, but that's the only element that's bolted down. 

Hard to believe it's 10 years already - we can't think of a better skeleton key to unlock the secrets behind Black Truffle's musical identity.

Finally, Kompakt issue a true GAS outlier on vinyl for the first time, recorded in 1989 and containing some of Wolfgang Voigt’s earliest and starkest recycling of magisterial Wagner loops, closest to the ends of The Caretaker, Philip Jeck, Kevin Drumm.

One of those releases that has lurked on our shelves since 2008 as a book and CD, ‘November 89’ exists in the margins of Wolfgang Voigt’s GAS canon as its creepiest and most occluded evocation of long walks in the Bavarian forests. While other GAS classics ooze a sort of dappled warmth breaking thru the trees in their widescreen dub techno strolls, you can fully feel the light dying over the horizon and the forest drawing in on this particularly gloomy, hour-long suite. 

As the title suggests, it was mostly, remarkably, made in ’89, back when Voigt was finding his feet between techno, house and indie-pop, and nearly a decade before he co-founded Kompakt with Michael Mayer & Jürgen Paape - by which time he was a full-fledged rave dynamo as Love Inc. and myriad others notable projects. And, in that sense, it can be heard as his ‘Selected Ambient Works 89-95’ - or perhaps more pertinently with SAW II vibes - in his nascent attempt to chase the ambient dragon, which surely endures for its strangely nostalgic, unheimlich qualities.

An educated guess leads us to think the first three were made in ’89, taking in the nightfall scenery of smudged symphonic strings and icy crackle to ‘Der Wald’, plus the muddied bass waltz and spectral pall of ‘Das Moor’, thru the self-evidently titled centrepiece ‘1989-11-01’, bristling with a digitally iridescent dread. ‘Tal 90’ and ‘Nah Und Fern’, which shares its title with the 2008 boxset, were most likely made a little later, and find the wintry doom thawing to the GAS-eous forms we’ve all come to deeply know and adore. 

A true evergreen for deep ambient techno connoisseurs, no less

Numero dust off the wiry, angular new wave of Mikel Rouse’s Tirez Tirez; one time Another Side label mates of Arthur Russell, Parade Ground and Tuxedomoon, and support act for Talking Heads, sharing all of their panache for sophisticated songwriting and pert grooves, at best in the bossa shimmy of ‘Living in This Dream (I’m So Proud)’ and a light-headed title tune...

“Tirez Tirez was founded by Missouri native Mikel Rouse, and gave its first performance as the opening act for the rock band Talking Heads at a 1978 concert in Kansas City, Missouri. The band's initial line-up was Rouse (vocals/guitar), Rob Shepperson (drums) and Jeff Burk (bass). Tirez Tirez issued two very rare self-released LPs in their earliest days: No Double Bagging Necessary (1978) and Rush & Dissonance (1979). All three members of the group subsequently moved to New York City in 1979, and self-released their debut single ("Scattered"/"Scenery") in November of that year. The band's third album (1980's Etudes) was recorded in New York City, but it did not initially see a US release, and was at first only picked up for distribution by the tiny British independent label Object Music. The LP went on to sell a very respectable 2,000 copies in the UK, and US indie Aura Records later issued in the album in the US in late 1981. Aura also issued "Razorblades", a single taken from the album.

Bassist Burk left Tirez Tirez in 1982, and was replaced by James Bergman. Philip Johnston (keyboards/woodwinds) was also added to the group at about the same time. This line-up (Rouse/Shepperson/Bergman/Johnston) recorded 1983's Story Of The Year, which was released only in Europe via Belgian label Les Disques Du Crépuscule. Although he had left Tirez Tirez, original band member Burk would continue to contribute finished artwork to future Tirez Tirez album and single releases after his 1982 departure; the same would be true of original drummer Shepperson after his departure in early 1984.”

‘hej!’ is the hauntingly hyperreal first album proper by Felicita, for PC Music.

Arriving 5 years since Felicita’s beguiling ‘(>’.’)>#’ and ‘Frenemies’ releases took us by surprise with their lacquered textures and uncannily poignant arrangements, ‘hej!’ claims their place in the same dimensions as Arca, Sophie and 0PN with a highly personalised expression of hyperreal modernity.

Polish folk, trance, trap and and classical chamber music are melded into the same mutant body of music with deceptively effortless appeal that’s both pop-wise and avant, charming and at times unsettling thru its juxtapositions of new and old. 

Warbling keys haunt much of the album, but in a way that swerves the poshness of, say Nils Frahm and co, for a more surreal and unreal effect, especially when he adds in snatches of processed Polish folk song, and then sharply switches to needling electronics, as with the vacuum sealed hyper reggaeton of ‘coughing up amber’, while the melodic couplet of ‘soft power I + II’ feel paradoxically timeless yet right in the pregnant here-and-now, though their pastoral field recordings came from a computer game, rather than the real thing.

The salty blatz of ’shook’ is a tart palate cleanser at the centre of the album, bristling with an outright aggression that contrast the rest of the set, particularly the eerie highlight of Caroline Polachek’s take on ‘marzipan’, an old Polish folk song reinterpreted with lustrous Reese-like bass and synthetic strings, while the sickening rush of ‘night soil (fade out)’ recalls the devil in the detail noise of Croww, and the closing ‘Mosaic’ elicits a most curious synthesis of emotions - ecstasy, fear, and romance in it’s fleeting choral cadence.

On a ravishing first LP in five years, Arca continues to assume her ultimate form - an HR Giger-esque biomechanical entity; a psychopomp between virtual, physical, and mythological worlds - hallucinating a posthuman club music that feels like the future manifest in her mastery of queer-coded Latin dance and electronic music vernacular.

Leading on from the sprawling ‘Kick’ (2020-21) pentalogy, ‘XXXXX’ consolidates past and present Arca in a sheer vision of club possibilities. Within her 15 year catalogue, the 16-part album appears to balance the ruggedly bittersweet, exploratory spirit of 2013’s ‘&&&&&’ mixtape - a key touchstone of deconstructed dance music - with a more aggressive, yet romantic, thrust that’s emerged thru the ‘Kick’ volumes. Coupled with an ever-finer grasp of the advanced electronica practised by Æ or AFX (or E+E & T C F) which has long underlined her work, and the experience of sharpening her pop talons on Madonna, Rosalía and Kelela records, the results come to light as self-contained album of multitudes, bursting at the seams with fresh yet timeless ideas. 

With the benefit of hindsight it’s not hard to cite Arca as a pied piper of hyper-contemporary electronic music, one instrumental in altering its prevailing rhythmic currency to sexier tresillo permutations, whilst bringing back notions of alien pop in a lineage harking to Bowie via SOPHIE - metaphorically disrupting the status quo and physically changing the way people dance, and both on a really significant scale. ‘XXXXX’ now binds and frays all those strands in her most sharply defined and digestible album statement, eliciting a spectra of emotional responses and proprioceptive sensation with visionary tact and immersive sound design tekkerz.

Geared with a metric, melodic, and spatial freedom that owes to classical music as much as ‘90s electronica and 2010s DAW hyperprisms, the 16 parts unfold from theatric spectralism of ‘No End’, thru the gothic dembow deathknells of ‘Willow’ and fleet hoofed hyperpop of ‘Eidolon’ into singular takes on depth-charged doble paso reggaeton in ’Syncope’, and shearing Ae lines of extended melodic thought on ‘Raver’. A brisk centrepiece ‘Fxck’ is the LP’s horny club anthem in waiting, whilst ‘Finisher’ is maybe the freakier raver’s fave, for its tumultuous dramaturgy of tense strings and displaced braindance-drill trepanation, sharing a deadly torque with the scythe of ‘Grip’ and intense frisson delivered by the saccades of ‘Everything’. Knit with hyperpop prayer ‘Enraptured’, and symphony of harpys summoned on ’Sueño’, it all leaves us in no doubt that Arca is near the apex of her game here.

items.body:
Epic 16 hour François Bayle retrospective, an unparalleled document of the key C.20th electro-acoustic and concrète pioneer and director of the hugely influential GRM institution from 1966-1997, where he was instrumental in bringing the Acousmonium speaker array and INA-GRM label to life, among many important, enduring innovations

This 10 year reissue of ’50 Ans d’Acousmagique’ joins INA-GRM’s quintessential boxsets of Pierre Schaeffer, Pierre Henry, Parmegiani, Radigue, and Xenakis in a rare, stellar microcosm of works by twentieth century groundbreakers. At 16 hrs long, and including 228 tracks, it offers a comprehensive overview of François Bayle’s unfathomable catalogue of work between 1972-2012. During this time Bayle was pivotal in altering perceptions of music’s materiality and purpose at the most fundamental and philosophic levels through his work in developing the Acousmonium diffusion system - an “orchestra of loudspeakers” which has become key to the GRM’s facilities in Paris - as well as supporting technological developments (Syter, GRM Tools, Midi Formers, Acousmographe) which are vital to his own remarkable compositions, and his endeavours organising radio broadcasts and events. 

Deeply informing and paralleling the history of recorded electronic music during its formative golden years, Bayle’s recordings render an embarrassment of riches for the discerning and explorative listener and historians of vanguard C.20th music. Between the flighty electro-acoustic staging of his avian dreams on ’72’s ‘Trois Rêves D'oiseau’ to the sensually lathered cosmic delirium of 1978-80’s ‘Erosphère’ works, to his beguiling latter tributes to his tutors at the Paris Conservatoire and Darmstadt summer courses, Messiaen and Stockhausen; the overwhelming scope of Bayle’s work, and thus the boxset, is brought into clearer focus by its chronological sequencing, offering a logical pathway thru his incredible projections of imagination.

It bears reflection that figures such as François Bayle created, and then opened, doors of perception for music in the past century that have come to mirror and shape the soundsphere we now inhabit. His innovations in sound spatialisation and the embrace of an acoustic unknown, or acousmagique, underline some of the most fascinating expressions of pathos thru art in our lifetimes, and this boxset is more than enough to send heads reeling into deep time for eons to come.

Breezy new age house by an Antipodean artist with illustrious credits beside Michal Hutchence, Bono, Jamiroquai since the ‘80s, evened out with Kuniyuki and 451 remixes...

"Originally emerging from Melbourne’s post-punk and new wave underground in the late 1970s and early 1980s, Gus Till has spent more than four decades navigating a remarkably diverse musical path. From early electronic experimentation with Third Eye alongside Ollie Olsen, through a pivotal role in the formative years of the global psy-trance movement and collaborations with artists including Michael Hutchence, System 7, Manu Dibango, Todd Terry and Bim Sherman, Till’s work has consistently resisted easy categorisation, moving fluidly between ambient music, downtempo, house, trance and psychedelic electronica.

First released on Japan’s Dakini Records in 2006, ‘Rainsong’ captures many of these threads in a single expansive composition. Built around a pulsating bassline, layered live percussion and soaring vocal elements, the track sits comfortably between the dancefloor and more immersive listening environments. Unfolding patiently across nearly thirteen minutes, it combines hypnotic rhythmic momentum with a rich sense of atmosphere and musicality.

For the B-side, Kuniyuki Takahashi offers a distinct reinterpretation of the original. His remix gradually unfolds from a patient introduction into a deep and richly textured exploration of the track’s core themes. Subtle spatial processing, nuanced arrangement shifts and his unmistakable sense of atmosphere transform the source material while preserving its emotional core."

items.body:
Following 2024's avant-prog-Americana song cycle 'Viewfinder', guitar deity Wendy Eisenberg goes chamber pop on their self-titled latest, tipping their hat to Judee Sill, Gillian Welch, Van Dyke Parks and Joanna Newsom.

When they relocated from rural Western Mass to Brooklyn in 2020, Eisenberg was hit with a wave of longing for the open landscape they'd left behind. They were drawn to classic country and folk records, perfectly poised offerings from Willie Nelson and John Hartford and lavish pop-folk records from Jimmy Webb and Van Dyke Parks as well as the weirdo fare of Richard Dawson et al. So when 'Viewfinder', a way of deconstructing the experience following eye surgery in 2011, was finished, Eisenberg started writing "genuinely folk songs" and swapping out their usually showy, complex performance for a form of relative simplicity that they explain is inherently strange all the same. Prog becomes folk, basically. And they're not on their own; more eaze handles the lush string arrangements, playing pedal steel and synthesizer, and a loose band forms around that axis, with drummer Ryan Sawyer and bassist Trevor Dunn.

But despite the personnel, it's resolutely Eisenberg's album. Their voice sounds unrestrained, capturing the era they're referencing and their own emotional (and physical upheaval). It's fragile but strangely warm on the country-tinged Jim O'Rourke-like 'Will You Dare' and hypnotic on the baroque 'Meaning Business', a track they wrote in the wake of David Lynch's death as the antithesis of the "Lynchian" aesthetic. And they should really get their flowers for this one; Americana, especially now, is teetering on a precipice, almost knocked off the edge by half-assed, churned attempts and underwritten pastiches. Eisenberg's an attentive listener and someone who's surrounded themself with similarly sensitive ears, people who are able to fill their heart and their sound so what we hear is as byzantine as a Gastr del Sol record but sounds as effortless as John Prine's 'Angel From Montgomery'. If you loved Joanna Newsom's 'Ys' and have never found anything quite as satisfying, this is the one.

items.body:
12th Isle push the boat out to Rosso Polare’s uchronic folklore, pulling from the Milanese artist’s Italian folk heritage and weaving in chops by Persian electro-acoustic artist Cinna Peyghamy, plus Italian avant-garde veteran Riccardo Sinigaglia, for an adventurous session braiding folk and concrète timelines... 

“Cacciamali is an exploration of diegetic sound, folk chants and traditional rhythms and instrumentation building upon Milan based Rosso Polare’s last outing Campo Amaro and the subsequent departure of co-founder Anna Vezzosi from the group. Where the 2024 album incorporated a heavy use of folklore as a new tool, Cacciamali explores the influence further by bringing in a host of collaborative players including Italian avant-garde veteran Riccardo Sinigaglia, sound artist and researcher HMOT (Stas Shärifulla) and Persian/Parisian electro-acoustic musician Cinna Peyghamy.

‘Scoff Back Sickness’, as the title loosely translates, utilises the same approach, one based on non-hierarchical authorship and leaning heavily on field recordings that both contrast and blend with the tonal material, focusing on biophony, landscape and environmental audio as compositional material. Shifting closer now to a shared network of voices and materials, the dual narrative unfolds as such:

Side A is connected to the concept of the medieval quintain games, specifically flag throwing, where certain drumming patterns from the tradition have been overworked, distorted and transformed. Side B is an underlying local legend from the north of Italy, where some sources speak of a presumed duel in 1744 between a father and his son, ultimately ending with the son’s death. These two layers are not illustrative but structural: ritual / repetition / tradition on one side, and rupture / conflict / loss on the other. A struggle to keep floating, a long shout in the distance, suspended between memory, ritual and disappearance. The result is dense, thick with impulse yet also measured, and often leaves us disoriented and questioning a sound's origin the moment we think we have a grip on the process. The gentle nostalgia of close-mic’ed ‘Falò’ summons the spirit of René Aubry & Jean Schwarz’s concréte masterpiece ‘Five Women’ on the Still Waters ballet soundtrack, and the stark contrast of looping rhythms on both ‘Xiv - Pavo’ and ‘Monte’ deploys a driving, intentful break from the moments of worldly human interactions served by the field recordings.”

items.body:
Not the birth of acid house, but a thrilling piece of synth raga set to brisk disco beats, Bollywood soundtrack composer Charanjit Singh’s ’82 LP is simply a landmark in its own right, and a proper ‘floor-filler to boot.

Since its first reissue in 2010, Singh’s cult, early use of the TB-303 on driving machine beats has been erroneously hailed the birth of acid house. OK the formula is there, but Chris Carter’s ‘Spaces Between’ (1980) and his CTI jam ‘Dancing Ghosts’ got there a couple of years before Singh, at the very least, and neither really inform the genius of Phuture and co a few years later. In any event, ‘Synthesizing: Ten Ragas To A Disco Beat’ is just an incredibly fruity boost to any club, revolving 10 hypnotic, pulsating jams closer to early Irdial (say, Aqua Regia’s ‘Hot Love’) than owt from the Chi. 

Taking a minute away from knocking out Bollywood scores and leading his wedding band covering popular songs, Singh would land upon a stroke of genius with ‘Ten Ragas To A Disco Beat’, finding the sweetspot between prevailing hi-NRG disco and millennia of raga traditions that patently transcended the sum of their parts more than 40 years later. It sounds very much of its time, rather than the stripped back linearity of later acid house, evidenced in the florid keyboard urges of ‘Raga Bhupali’, transposing a steamy sort of club canter to somewhere even more humid.

A real club evergreen, suck it and see.
